content.title: Dangerous Fake Microsoft Windows Update Confirmed—Do Not Download
content.text: Do not download this fake Microsoft Windows update.NurPhoto via Getty ImagesUpdate April 16: Following confirmation of a highly dangerous fake Windows Update that users have been warned not to download, this article has been revised to include: information regarding the second-largest Patch Tuesday security vulnerability update ever, which Microsoft users really must install to ensure their Windows systems are properly protected against attack, along with details of an April Windows Server security update that some users are finding they cannot install even though they want to. Don’t be confused. Be informed and stay safe.When it comes to staying on top of your security, it can be an uphill climb for Microsoft Windows users sometimes. Dozens, sometimes hundreds, of new vulnerabilities are confirmed on the second Tuesday of every month, new malware to deal with and now comes the news that a fake Windows update is stealing account passwords, payment data and more.With security updates being such an important part of the risk-reduction process, when malicious copies are introduced into the mix, they not only harm those who download them but might also deter others from installing the genuine item for fear of attack. Here’s what you need to know and do about malicious Microsoft support websites and associated dangerous downloads. ForbesGoogle Chrome Users Warned As Hackers Target Gmail And YouTube UsersFake Microsoft Windows Update Steals Data And Terminates Security ToolsIt’s been a minute since I last warned about dangerous Microsoft Windows security updates that were actually nothing of the sort. But the threat has certainly not gone away, and with billions of people using various Windows operating systems, why would it? The latest warning comes courtesy of Stefan Dasic, a cybersecurity and malware researcher at Malwarebytes, who has published a highly detailed technical analysis concerning malware that is being distributed by a fake Microsoft support site and is wrapped up within what appears to be a legitimate cumulative update for Windows version 24H2, complete with a believable knowledge base article number. “Because the file looks legitimate and avoids detection,” Dasic said, “it can slip past both users and security tools.”The fake Windows website appears to have been specifically targeting French Microsoft users, but as Dasic warned, “these campaigns tend to spread quickly.” All users, regardless of nationality, are therefore urged to take note and be aware of the threat posed by this and similar attacks.ForbesMicrosoft Confirms New And Widespread 2FA Code Attacks OngoingBy Davey Winder While reading the full analysis is recommended for those of a technical bent, the bullet point version is as follows:MoreSettingsFull Screen (F)Play (SPACE)Read More (Shift + O) 360p 720p HD1080p HDAuto(360p) V324082750 Visit Advertiser websiteGO TO PAGEThe threat is delivered via social engineering, requiring the victim to click a link to reach the fake Microsoft support website.The malware is dressed up as a cumulative Windows 24H2 update; its file properties are carefully spoofed down to the comments filed claiming it contains “the logic and data required to install WindowsUpdate.”Do Not Ignore This New Microsoft Windows Update, Here’s Why And How To Install It Safely As mentioned earlier, the second Tuesday of the month sees Microsoft release patches for Windows vulnerabilities and other issues that affect users. The April Patch Tuesday rollout has now dropped, and it’s critical that you don’t ignore it.Here’s why, by the numbers:A total of 167 security issues have been addressed.Amongst this number are two zero-day vulnerabilities.Eight of the vulnerabilities patched have a critical severity rating.Seven of them involve remote code execution as the payload danger of successful exploitation.This is the highest number of vulnerabilities patched by Microsoft so far this year, up by 88 over last month. It is also the second-highest number of vulnerabilities ever fixed since the Patch Tuesday rollouts started back in October 2003. It has only, and only just for that matter, been beaten by the 167 Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures back in October 2025. “At this pace,” Satnam Narang, a senior staff research engineer at Tenable, said, “2026 is on track to affirm that 1,000+ Patch Tuesday CVEs annually is the norm." This could, of course, be influenced by the increasing use of AI by both internal processes and external security researchers when hunting for security issues in operating systems and other software. Whatever the reason, it remains a good thing. Far better to know about vulnerabilities and get them patched than have threat actors find them and use them before a vendor and its customers can do so. “Microsoft is aware of exploitation in the wild for one of today’s vulnerabilities, and public disclosure for one other,” Adam Barnett, a principal software engineer at Rapid7, said.Meanwhile, Tyler Reguly, an associate director of security research and development at Fortra, told me that “there are 19 vulnerabilities listed as Exploitation More Likely. In the first quarter of the year, we saw 20 vulnerabilities listed as Exploitation More Likely and now, in a single month, we’re seeing only one less than that total. That is something to pay attention to, especially given the nature of the services affected.”The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, better known by the acronym CISA, has now added both zero-days, CVE-2009-0238 (Microsoft Office Remote Code Execution Vulnerability) and CVE-2026-32201 (Microsoft SharePoint Server Improper Input Validation Vulnerability) to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. ForbesAngry Hacker Drops Microsoft Zero-Day Exploit, 1 Billion Users WarnedBy Davey WinderAll of which means that sitting back and doing nothing isn’t really an option for consumers, at least. Enterprise users will, of course, be applying updates according to their organization’s risk and patch management processes. “The elevated number of patches, combined with the presence of zero-days and multiple critical issues,” Jack Bicer, director of vulnerability research at Action1, said, “makes this a release that should be prioritized for immediate attention.”Microsoft Windows Server KB5082063 Security Update Fails To Install For Some UsersSometimes, installing a genuine, legitimate and essential security update for Windows isn’t all plain sailing. Such is the case, it would appear, with the April KB5082063 security update for users of Windows Server 2025. Microsoft MVP Susan Bradley has published a Microsoft service alert confirmation that stated “Microsoft is monitoring diagnostic data reports on update installation failures and has observed a recurring error on Windows Server 2025 devices when installing the April 2026 Windows security update, released on April 14, 2026.” Microsoft said that a “limited number of affected servers” might experience an installation failure, which is accompanied by an error code of 800F0983, but it has not clarified what the affected numbers might be beyond that. The good news, I guess, is that Microsoft has said it is “actively investigating this issue and will provide more information as more details become available.” The bad news, of course, is that an essential security update is failing, yet again, for some users.Consumers Advised To Install Microsoft Security Patches Using The Windows Automatic Updates OptionAll Microsoft Windows users are urged to install updates only through Settings | Windows Update | Check for updates. Automatic updates exist for a reason, and they can greatly mitigate the chances of finding yourself on the end of a fake one. If you prefer manual updating, only ever do so through the official Microsoft Update Catalog and always access this directly through your browser. As I said right at the beginning of this article, be informed and don’t get confused. I appreciate that, given all that is happening in the world of social engineering attacks, combined with updates that don’t always work as they should, it can be something of a minefield. However, the security explosion that’s waiting to be triggered if you don’t update in a safe and timely fashion doesn’t bear thinking about.
